title: Robots Are Still at GPT-1, and the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
dek: The scaling-law signal for embodied intelligence has appeared, but the metric being measured is wrong: low loss does not mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
why: Xu Mengdi, assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and in-context learning for embodied intelligence; the middle and later sections on the data loop and the loss trap are the most valuable.
who: Founders, researchers and investors in embodied intelligence, especially anyone agonizing over data-collection routes, world models vs. VLA, and how to evaluate model progress.
skip: The opening rapid-fire Q&A and the Hengshui High School story can be skipped; go straight to the embodied-startup and data section after the 44-minute mark.

points.h: Pretraining is not everything; adaptation is what matters
points.body: Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is called Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you cannot hope a robot will succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The open world is defined by constantly changing tasks — a home has 20 objects today, a week later it has 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences change too. So the robot must be able to adapt to change and improve itself in the deployment environment. She explored two paths: in-context learning and test-time training, the latter changing only 0.5% of the adapter parameters, though changing more causes forgetting of pretrained knowledge.

points.h: Why adaptation only became important now
points.body: Humans generalize well for two reasons: an extremely strong prior, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — effectively giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this does not mean adaptation is unimportant — it is just that people only recently realized it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you do not want the robot's self-learning process in a real scenario to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

points.h: Low loss does not equal high success rate
points.body: This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There is a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate; loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low, and there will be a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps make no contact with the object; even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18, when contact actually happens, has a relatively large error, the task easily fails. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a meaningful scaling law should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

points.h: Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
points.body: The mainstream embodied model today is still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to achieve is the GPT-3 moment: through ICL, through prompting, giving the model task information without fine-tuning, telling the model what to do only through context. That way the weight of fine-tuning becomes weaker, it is easier to scale to more scenarios and complete more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

points.h: The data loop is a chicken-and-egg problem
points.body: The hardest point is whether the model can have a stable data loop. This requires putting the robot into end-user homes or service scenarios, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot must show obvious progress after being taught for half an hour, so that end users are willing to use it and the data loop can start turning. But there is a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to enter the scenario first so users start using it, in order to activate the base capability. So whether the data loop can be made to work is the riskiest point.

points.h: Data is defined by working backward from model capability
points.body: Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data is not conjured out of thin air; it is defined by the model's capability. When people define data, what they are actually doing is: working backward from what capability the model needs to how the data should be collected. For example, if smoother actions are needed, the data should be of the smooth type; if fail-recovery capability is needed, the data should be collected with failures and corrections. And right now everyone's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

points.h: Each of the four data types has its own place
points.body: Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body and suits the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily creates position generalization and texture generalization, making the model more robust to visual changes, and suits pretraining or the front end of mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest and can be spread widely across different scenarios; what it teaches is scene variation and task-related information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

points.h: AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
points.body: Robotics papers have recently been doubling in growth, and Xu Mengdi's response is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still will not be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar but in fact have many holes in their arguments and do not contain much. If she finds out an article was written by AI, her interest in it is discounted.

terms.def: Adapting a model to a new task through the context in the prompt without changing model parameters.
A model that maps vision and language instructions directly to robot actions.
A data-collection method between robot data and human data, with lower cost.
Model-agnostic meta-learning: letting a model learn to quickly adapt to unseen tasks; the opportunity that brought Xu Mengdi into the field.
DeepMind work arguing that model parameters are equivalent to an RL algorithm.
Once you choose a decision, you have to bear its weaker aspects.
